claim: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is the most common spine disorder affecting children worldwide.
source: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is the most common spine disorder affecting children worldwide, yet little is known about the pathogenesis of this disorder.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge about the prevalence of AIS.

claim: Little is known about the pathogenesis of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
source: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is the most common spine disorder affecting children worldwide, yet little is known about the pathogenesis of this disorder.
evidence: This is an assertion about the current state of scientific understanding.

claim: Genetic regulation of structural components of the axial skeleton, intervertebral discs, and dense connective tissues is essential for the maintenance of spinal alignment.
source: Here, we demonstrate that genetic regulation of structural components of the axial skeleton, the intervertebral discs, and dense connective tissues (i.e., ligaments and tendons) is essential for the maintenance of spinal alignment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript using various mouse models.

claim: ADGRG6 was previously implicated in human AIS association studies.
source: We show that the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor ADGRG6, previously implicated in human AIS association studies, is required in these tissues to maintain typical spine alignment in mice.
evidence: This refers to prior published research linking ADGRG6 to AIS.

claim: ADGRG6 is required in the axial skeleton, intervertebral discs, and dense connective tissues to maintain typical spine alignment in mice.
source: We show that the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor ADGRG6, previously implicated in human AIS association studies, is required in these tissues to maintain typical spine alignment in mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from conditional knockout mice presented in the manuscript.

claim: ADGRG6 regulates biomechanical properties of tendon.
source: Furthermore, we show that ADGRG6 regulates biomechanical properties of tendon and stimulates CREB signaling governing gene expression in cartilaginous tissues of the spine.
evidence: This is supported by mechanical testing data presented in Figure 7.

claim: ADGRG6 stimulates CREB signaling governing gene expression in cartilaginous tissues of the spine.
source: Furthermore, we show that ADGRG6 regulates biomechanical properties of tendon and stimulates CREB signaling governing gene expression in cartilaginous tissues of the spine.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and western blot data showing reduced pCREB in mutant tissues.

claim: Treatment with a cAMP agonist can mirror aspects of ADGRG6 receptor function in culture.
source: Treatment with a cAMP agonist could mirror aspects of receptor function in culture, thus defining core pathways for regulating these axial cartilaginous and connective tissues.
evidence: This is supported by forskolin treatment experiments in ATDC5 cells shown in Figure 4.

claim: ADGRG6 is a key gene involved in human AIS.
source: As ADGRG6 is a key gene involved in human AIS, these findings open up novel therapeutic opportunities for human scoliosis.
evidence: This is based on genome-wide association studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The findings open up novel therapeutic opportunities for human scoliosis.
source: As ADGRG6 is a key gene involved in human AIS, these findings open up novel therapeutic opportunities for human scoliosis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications based on the research findings.

claim: The spine consists of segmented bony vertebral bodies linked together by fibrocartilaginous joints named the intervertebral discs (IVDs).
source: The spine consists of a series of segmented bony vertebral bodies linked together by fibrocartilaginous joints named the intervertebral discs (IVDs), which aid in lateral and rotational flexibility and cushioning loading of the spinal column.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Intervertebral discs aid in lateral and rotational flexibility and cushioning loading of the spinal column.
source: The spine consists of a series of segmented bony vertebral bodies linked together by fibrocartilaginous joints named the intervertebral discs (IVDs), which aid in lateral and rotational flexibility and cushioning loading of the spinal column.
evidence: This is established anatomical and biomechanical knowledge.

claim: The spine is supported by paraspinal ligaments.
source: The spine is further supported by the paraspinal ligaments and provides attachment sites for multiple muscle-tendon insertions.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The spine provides attachment sites for multiple muscle-tendon insertions.
source: The spine is further supported by the paraspinal ligaments and provides attachment sites for multiple muscle-tendon insertions.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The structural organization of the axial skeleton aids in the protection of the spinal cord.
source: Finally, the structural organization of the axial skeleton aids in the protection of the spinal cord and acts as the central axis of the body to support and maintain posture during movement through the environment (Bagnat and Gray, 2020; Bogduk, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited references on spinal anatomy and function.

claim: The axial skeleton acts as the central axis of the body to support and maintain posture during movement through the environment.
source: Finally, the structural organization of the axial skeleton aids in the protection of the spinal cord and acts as the central axis of the body to support and maintain posture during movement through the environment (Bagnat and Gray, 2020; Bogduk, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited references on spinal anatomy and function.

claim: Scoliosis is commonly diagnosed by a lateral curvature of 10° or greater in the coronal plane.
source: Scoliosis is a complex rotational atypical configuration of the spine, commonly diagnosed by a lateral curvature of 10° or greater in the coronal plane (Cheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a clinical definition supported by a citation.

claim: Scoliosis can be caused by congenital patterning defects of the vertebral column.
source: Scoliosis can be caused by congenital patterning defects of the vertebral column or associated with various neuromuscular or syndromic disorders (Murphy and Mooney, 2019).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Scoliosis can be associated with various neuromuscular or syndromic disorders.
source: Scoliosis can be caused by congenital patterning defects of the vertebral column or associated with various neuromuscular or syndromic disorders (Murphy and Mooney, 2019).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Idiopathic scoliosis occurs in otherwise healthy children without associated patterning or neuromuscular conditions.
source: In contrast, idiopathic scoliosis occurs in otherwise healthy children without associated patterning or neuromuscular conditions.
evidence: This is a clinical definition distinguishing idiopathic from other forms of scoliosis.

claim: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis affects approximately 3% of children worldwide.
source: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is the most common pediatric spine disorder, affecting ~3% of children worldwide (Cheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an epidemiological statistic supported by a citation.

claim: Surgical correction for AIS aims to halt the progression of severe curves.
source: Clinical interventions for AIS include surgical correction, which aims to halt the progression of severe curves, but which places a high socioeconomic burden on patients and families (Negrini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Surgical correction for AIS places a high socioeconomic burden on patients and families.
source: Clinical interventions for AIS include surgical correction, which aims to halt the progression of severe curves, but which places a high socioeconomic burden on patients and families (Negrini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation discussing clinical interventions.

claim: The molecular genetics and pathology underlying AIS remain ill-defined.
source: Despite substantial efforts to decipher the pathogenesis of AIS, the molecular genetics and pathology underlying this condition remain ill-defined (Cheng et al., 2015; Newton Ede and Jones, 2016).
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The appearance of spine curvatures in AIS patients without obvious morphological defects suggests that subtle defects in regulators of spine stability may contribute to the pathogenesis.
source: The appearance of spine curvatures in AIS patients without obvious morphological defects of the vertebral column suggests that more subtle defects in one or more regulators of spine stability may contribute to the pathogenesis of this disorder.
evidence: This is an inference based on clinical observations.

claim: Subtle asymmetric morphological changes of the vertebral bodies at the apical region of the curve have been observed in some AIS patients.
source: Indeed, subtle asymmetric morphological changes of the vertebral bodies at the apical region of the curve have been observed in some AIS patients, which may initiate spine curvature (Lam et al., 2011; Liljenqvist et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Asymmetric morphological changes of vertebral bodies may initiate spine curvature in AIS patients.
source: Indeed, subtle asymmetric morphological changes of the vertebral bodies at the apical region of the curve have been observed in some AIS patients, which may initiate spine curvature (Lam et al., 2011; Liljenqvist et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited observations.

claim: Changes in cell density and glycosaminoglycan composition in IVDs have been observed in AIS patients.
source: In addition, changes in cell density and glycosaminoglycan composition (Shu and Melrose, 2018; Urban et al., 2001), altered ultrastructure of collagen and elastic fibers (Akhtar et al., 2005), and increased incidence of endplate-oriented disc herniations (i.e., Schmorl's nodes) (Buttermann and Mullin, 2008) may also contribute to the onset of scoliosis in AIS patients.
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Altered ultrastructure of collagen and elastic fibers has been observed in AIS patients.
source: In addition, changes in cell density and glycosaminoglycan composition (Shu and Melrose, 2018; Urban et al., 2001), altered ultrastructure of collagen and elastic fibers (Akhtar et al., 2005), and increased incidence of endplate-oriented disc herniations (i.e., Schmorl's nodes) (Buttermann and Mullin, 2008) may also contribute to the onset of scoliosis in AIS patients.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical study.

claim: Increased incidence of endplate-oriented disc herniations (Schmorl's nodes) has been observed in AIS patients.
source: In addition, changes in cell density and glycosaminoglycan composition (Shu and Melrose, 2018; Urban et al., 2001), altered ultrastructure of collagen and elastic fibers (Akhtar et al., 2005), and increased incidence of endplate-oriented disc herniations (i.e., Schmorl's nodes) (Buttermann and Mullin, 2008) may also contribute to the onset of scoliosis in AIS patients.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical study.

claim: Genome-wide association studies and meta-analysis of multiethnic AIS cohorts strongly implicate the ADGRG6 gene for susceptibility to scoliosis.
source: Genome-wide association studies and subsequent meta-analysis of multiethnic AIS cohorts strongly implicate the ADGRG6 gene for susceptibility to scoliosis (Kou et al., 2013; Kou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: ADGRG6 is a member of the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor family of proteins.
source: ADGRG6 (also called GPR126) is a member of the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor family of proteins, many of which display canonical intercellular signaling function via activation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) (Hamann et al., 2015; Langenhan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established molecular biology knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Many adhesion G protein-coupled receptors display canonical intercellular signaling function via activation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).
source: ADGRG6 (also called GPR126) is a member of the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor family of proteins, many of which display canonical intercellular signaling function via activation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) (Hamann et al., 2015; Langenhan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established molecular biology knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ADGRG6 functions through canonical cAMP signaling to regulate Schwann cell differentiation and myelination.
source: In addition, ADGRG6 has been shown to function through canonical cAMP signaling to regulate Schwann cell differentiation and myelination and the regulation of inner ear development (Geng et al., 2013; Monk et al., 2009; Monk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ADGRG6 functions through canonical cAMP signaling to regulate inner ear development.
source: In addition, ADGRG6 has been shown to function through canonical cAMP signaling to regulate Schwann cell differentiation and myelination and the regulation of inner ear development (Geng et al., 2013; Monk et al., 2009; Monk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adgrg6 null mutant mice are embryonic lethal.
source: Adgrg6 null mutant mice are embryonic lethal, with a few survivors displaying cardiac defects and severe joint contractures, but die before weaning (Mogha et al., 2013; Monk et al., 2011; Waller-Evans et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior mouse studies.

claim: A few Adgrg6 null mutant mice survivors display cardiac defects and severe joint contractures but die before weaning.
source: Adgrg6 null mutant mice are embryonic lethal, with a few survivors displaying cardiac defects and severe joint contractures, but die before weaning (Mogha et al., 2013; Monk et al., 2011; Waller-Evans et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior mouse studies.

claim: Conditional ablation of Adgrg6 in osteochondral progenitor cells generated a reproducible genetic mouse model that displayed postnatal-onset scoliosis without causing obvious patterning defects of the vertebral column.
source: However, conditional ablation of Adgrg6 in osteochondral progenitor cells generated a reproducible genetic mouse model that displayed postnatal-onset scoliosis without causing obvious patterning defects of the vertebral column (Karner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Adgrg6 is expressed in the vertebral growth plate, nucleus pulposus, and cartilaginous endplate in neonatal mouse spine.
source: To address the pathogenesis of AIS observed in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice, we first assayed the expression pattern of Adgrg6 in neonatal mouse spine using fluorescent in situ hybridization, which showed expression in the vertebral growth plate, nucleus pulposus, and the cartilaginous endplate (Figure 1A–C'').
evidence: This is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Col2a1-Cre targets nucleus pulposus, annulus fibrosus, endplate, and growth plate at both P1 and P28.
source: β-galactosidase staining of Col2a1-Cre; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ spine sections at P1 (E, E') and P28 (F, F'). Col2a1-Cre targets NP, AF, EP, and GP, as well as some cells in the bony tissues at both P1 and P28.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1E-F'.

claim: Col2a1-Cre targets some cells in bony tissues at both P1 and P28.
source: β-galactosidase staining of Col2a1-Cre; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ spine sections at P1 (E, E') and P28 (F, F'). Col2a1-Cre targets NP, AF, EP, and GP, as well as some cells in the bony tissues at both P1 and P28.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1E-F'.

claim: Col2a1-Cre targets the outermost annulus fibrosus at P28.
source: Note that Col2a1-Cre also targets the outmost AF (black arrows, F') and the periosteum (Po) (green arrows, F') at P28.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1F'.

claim: Col2a1-Cre targets the periosteum at P28.
source: Note that Col2a1-Cre also targets the outmost AF (black arrows, F') and the periosteum (Po) (green arrows, F') at P28.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1F'.

claim: Bglap-Cre targets trabecular bone at P1.
source: β-Galactosidase staining of Bglap-Cre; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ spine sections at P1 (G, G') and P28 (H, H'). Bglap-Cre targets TB at P1 (G, G'), but targets TB (H'), CB (H'), and Po (green arrows, H') at P28.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1G-G'.

claim: Bglap-Cre targets trabecular bone, cortical bone, and periosteum at P28.
source: β-Galactosidase staining of Bglap-Cre; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ spine sections at P1 (G, G') and P28 (H, H'). Bglap-Cre targets TB at P1 (G, G'), but targets TB (H'), CB (H'), and Po (green arrows, H') at P28.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1H-H'.

claim: Bglap-Cre targets hypertrophic cells within the endplate and growth plate at P28.
source: Bglap-Cre also targets hypertrophic cells within the EP and GP (H').
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1H'.

claim: ATC targets most cells in nucleus pulposus, annulus fibrosus, endplate, and growth plate at both P1 and P28 when induced from E0.5-P20.
source: β-Galactosidase staining of ATC; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ (Dox-induced from E0.5–P20) spine sections at P1 (I, I') and P28 (J, J'). ATC targets most cells in NP, AF, EP, and GP at both time points.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1I-J'.

claim: ATC does not target the outermost annulus fibrosus when induced from E0.5-P20.
source: Note that ATC did not target the outmost AF (black dash line and arrows, J'), nor the Po (green arrows, J').
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1J'.

claim: ATC does not target the periosteum when induced from E0.5-P20.
source: Note that ATC did not target the outmost AF (black dash line and arrows, J'), nor the Po (green arrows, J').
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1J'.

claim: Scx-Cre targets annulus fibrosus at P1 and P28.
source: β-Galactosidase staining of Scx-Cre; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ spine sections at P1 (K, K') and P28 (L, L'). Scx-Cre targets AF at P1 (K') and P28 (L'), and also recombines in several cells of NP, EP, and GP (L') at P28.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1K-L'.

claim: Scx-Cre recombines in several cells of nucleus pulposus, endplate, and growth plate at P28.
source: β-Galactosidase staining of Scx-Cre; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ spine sections at P1 (K, K') and P28 (L, L'). Scx-Cre targets AF at P1 (K') and P28 (L'), and also recombines in several cells of NP, EP, and GP (L') at P28.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1L'.

claim: Scx-Cre targets some cells of the outermost annulus fibrosus at P28.
source: Note that Scx-Cre also targets some cells of the outmost AF (black arrows, L') and the Po (green arrows, L') at P28.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1L'.

claim: Scx-Cre targets some cells of the periosteum at P28.
source: Note that Scx-Cre also targets some cells of the outmost AF (black arrows, L') and the Po (green arrows, L') at P28.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1L'.

claim: Col2a1-Cre recombines in supraspinous ligaments at P1.
source: Whole-mount β-galactosidase staining of a Col2a1-Cre; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ mouse at P1 showed that Col2a1-Cre also recombined in some dense connective tissues (i.e., ligaments and tendons) along the spine (Figure 1N, N'), such as the supraspinous ligaments flanking the spine (black arrows, Figure 1M', N').
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount β-galactosidase staining shown in Figure 1N-N'.

claim: Most cells in the supraspinous ligaments are LacZ positive in Col2a1-Cre; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ mice.
source: Coronal and transverse sections of the Col2a1-Cre; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ mouse spine showed that most cells in the supraspinous ligaments were LacZ positive (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–K), and IHC analyses on adjacent sections showed that these cells also expressed ADGRG6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H', I', and K').
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining and IHC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: LacZ positive cells in supraspinous ligaments also express ADGRG6.
source: Coronal and transverse sections of the Col2a1-Cre; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ mouse spine showed that most cells in the supraspinous ligaments were LacZ positive (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–K), and IHC analyses on adjacent sections showed that these cells also expressed ADGRG6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H', I', and K').
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ADGRG6 expression is significantly reduced in endplate and growth plate in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice at P20.
source: To understand the knockdown efficiency of Adgrg6 in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice, we performed IHC analyses and observed significantly reduced expression of ADGRG6 in endplate and growth plate in the mutant mice at P20 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: ADGRG6 expression is reduced in the annulus fibrosis of Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice at P20.
source: We also observed reduced expression in the annulus fibrosis of mutant mice (p=0.068, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), which was especially apparent in scoliotic individuals (p=0.0383, red dots; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice were indistinguishable from littermate controls at birth.
source: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice were indistinguishable from littermate controls at birth and displayed typical patterning and alignment of the spine at P10 (n = 23) (Figure 2E, E').
evidence: This is supported by X-ray data shown in Figure 2E-E'.

claim: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice displayed typical patterning and alignment of the spine at P10.
source: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice were indistinguishable from littermate controls at birth and displayed typical patterning and alignment of the spine at P10 (n = 23) (Figure 2E, E').
evidence: This is supported by X-ray data shown in Figure 2E-E'.

claim: Postnatal-onset spine curvatures were first observed in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice at P20.
source: However, at P20, we first observed postnatal-onset spine curvatures (Figure 2F, F'), which could be progressive in some Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f animals (Figure 2F–H').
evidence: This is supported by X-ray data shown in Figure 2F-F'.

claim: Spine curvatures could be progressive in some Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f animals.
source: However, at P20, we first observed postnatal-onset spine curvatures (Figure 2F, F'), which could be progressive in some Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f animals (Figure 2F–H').
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal X-ray data shown in Figure 2F-H'.

claim: Approximately 60% of Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice exhibited scoliosis at P20, P40, and P120.
source: Approximately 60% of Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice exhibited scoliosis at P20 (52.1%; n = 23), P40 (60.8%; n = 23), and P120 (58.8%; n = 17) (Figure 2I, K, L), with the apex of the curvature centered at thoracic vertebrae (T)8 and T9 (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by Cobb angle measurements shown in Figure 2I-L.

claim: The apex of the curvature in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice is centered at thoracic vertebrae T8 and T9.
source: Approximately 60% of Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice exhibited scoliosis at P20 (52.1%; n = 23), P40 (60.8%; n = 23), and P120 (58.8%; n = 17) (Figure 2I, K, L), with the apex of the curvature centered at thoracic vertebrae (T)8 and T9 (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by heat map analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The mean Cobb angle increased in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice compared with control littermates.
source: The mean Cobb angle increased in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice compared with control littermates (Figure 2I), ranging from 11° to 46° in scoliotic individuals (Figure 2I, L).
evidence: This is supported by Cobb angle measurements shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Cobb angles in scoliotic Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice ranged from 11° to 46°.
source: The mean Cobb angle increased in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice compared with control littermates (Figure 2I), ranging from 11° to 46° in scoliotic individuals (Figure 2I, L).
evidence: This is supported by Cobb angle measurements shown in Figure 2I, L.

claim: Only one Cre (+) control mouse had a mild curve of 13.8° at P120.
source: In comparison, only one Cre (+) control mouse (n = 18) had a mild curve of 13.8° at P120, with the remainder displaying no alteration in spine alignment (Figure 2I, K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Cobb angle measurements shown in Figure 2I, K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Scoliosis was observed in 37.5% of male and 66.6% of female Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice.
source: We observed scoliosis in both 37.5% (n = 8) of male and 66.6% (n = 15) of female mutant mice, with both right- or left-ward curvatures (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by Cobb angle measurements shown in Figure 2L.

claim: No obvious sex bias for the incidence of scoliosis was observed in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.
source: We did not observe an obvious sex bias for the incidence of scoliosis (Fisher exact test, p=0.2213).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Wedging of the vertebrae and IVD within regions of acute spine curvature is observed in human AIS.
source: Wedging of the vertebrae and the IVD within regions of acute spine curvature is observed in human AIS (Little et al., 2016; Newton Ede and Jones, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Wedging of IVDs close to the apex of the curvature was observed in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice with scoliosis at P20.
source: During the initiation of scoliosis (P20), we observed wedging of IVDs close to the apex of the curvature in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice with scoliosis, associated with a shift of the nucleus pulposus towards the convexity of the curve (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Wedging of IVDs in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice was associated with a shift of the nucleus pulposus towards the convexity of the curve.
source: During the initiation of scoliosis (P20), we observed wedging of IVDs close to the apex of the curvature in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice with scoliosis, associated with a shift of the nucleus pulposus towards the convexity of the curve (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Large vacuolated cells (notochordal cells) shifted towards the convex side in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice with scoliosis.
source: The large vacuolated cells (magenta stained/notochordal cells) shifted towards the convex side, while the smaller non-vacuolated cells (blue-stained/chondrocyte-like cells) distributed in the middle and concave side (Figure 3B, B''), in contrast to the uniform distribution of these cells with the IVD typical of control littermates (Figure 3A, A'').
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3B-B''.

claim: Smaller non-vacuolated cells (chondrocyte-like cells) distributed in the middle and concave side in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice with scoliosis.
source: The large vacuolated cells (magenta stained/notochordal cells) shifted towards the convex side, while the smaller non-vacuolated cells (blue-stained/chondrocyte-like cells) distributed in the middle and concave side (Figure 3B, B''), in contrast to the uniform distribution of these cells with the IVD typical of control littermates (Figure 3A, A'').
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3B-B''.

claim: More vertical alignment of the annulus fibrosis lamellae was observed in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice along the convex side.
source: We observed more vertical alignment of the annulus fibrosis lamellae in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice along the convex side (white dash lines, Figure 3A', B'), with flatter lamellae and an elongated inner annulus fibrosus at the concave side the IVD (white dash lines, Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A'-B'.

claim: Flatter lamellae and an elongated inner annulus fibrosus were observed at the concave side of the IVD in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.
source: We observed more vertical alignment of the annulus fibrosis lamellae in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice along the convex side (white dash lines, Figure 3A', B'), with flatter lamellae and an elongated inner annulus fibrosus at the concave side the IVD (white dash lines, Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Older Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f scoliotic mice (P120) showed a more pronounced shift of the nucleus pulposus to the convex side.
source: Older Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f scoliotic mice (P120) showed a more pronounced shift of the nucleus pulposus to the convex side (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, D''), with vertical alignment of the annulus fibrosus lamellae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, D') and the endplate and growth plate tissues appeared thinner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C''', D''').
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-D''.

claim: The endplate and growth plate tissues appeared thinner in older Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f scoliotic mice (P120).
source: Older Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f scoliotic mice (P120) showed a more pronounced shift of the nucleus pulposus to the convex side (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, D''), with vertical alignment of the annulus fibrosus lamellae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, D') and the endplate and growth plate tissues appeared thinner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C''', D''').
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C'''-D'''.

claim: No obvious histopathology was observed in the cartilaginous endplate and vertebral growth plate in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice at P20.
source: Analysis of the cartilaginous endplate and the vertebral growth plate in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice showed no obvious histopathology at P20 (Figure 3A, A''', B, B''').
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A-B'''.

claim: No apparent defects in the size or patterning of the vertebrae, growth plates, or IVD tissues were observed during the initiation of scoliosis at P20 in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.
source: Despite wedging of IVDs close to the apex of the curvature in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice, no apparent defects in the size or patterning of the vertebrae, growth plates, or IVD tissues were observed during the initiation of scoliosis at P20 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B), nor prior to the onset of scoliosis at P10 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F'').
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Bulging of the cortical bone outward on the concave side of the curve was occasionally observed at P20 in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.
source: However, we occasionally observed bulging of the cortical bone outward on the concave side of the curve at P20 (50%; n = 4; black arrow, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IVDs lying proximal or distal to prominent spine curvatures in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice exhibited typical nucleus pulposus and annulus fibrosus tissues.
source: Interestingly, the IVDs lying proximal or distal to prominent spine curvatures in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice exhibited typical nucleus pulposus and annulus fibrosus tissues compared with littermate control tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A', B'), suggesting that local unbalance of forces at the thoracic spine drives the alterations in tissue architecture.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A'-B'.

claim: Local unbalance of forces at the thoracic spine drives the alterations in tissue architecture in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.
source: Interestingly, the IVDs lying proximal or distal to prominent spine curvatures in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice exhibited typical nucleus pulposus and annulus fibrosus tissues compared with littermate control tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A', B'), suggesting that local unbalance of forces at the thoracic spine drives the alterations in tissue architecture.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that only IVDs near the curve show alterations.

claim: Analysis of the IVD and growth plate in human AIS patients has demonstrated cellularity alterations, changes in gene expression, and reduced proteoglycan content.
source: Analysis of the IVD and growth plate in human AIS patients has demonstrated cellularity alterations, changes in the typical expression of anabolic and catabolic genes, and reduced proteoglycan content (Newton Ede and Jones, 2016; Roberts et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant IVD tissue demonstrated altered regulation of Sox5, Sox6, and Sox9 genes.
source: Analysis of the transcriptional and epigenetic changes in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant IVD tissue demonstrated altered regulation of several anabolic factors and extracellular matrix (ECM) components expressed in healthy cartilaginous tissues, including Sox5, Sox6, and Sox9 genes (Liu et al., 2019; Makki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SOX9 is an essential transcriptional regulator of cartilage and IVD homeostasis in mouse.
source: We assayed SOX9, an essential transcriptional regulator of cartilage and IVD homeostasis in mouse (Henry et al., 2012), which showed strong expression throughout the IVD in littermate control mouse spine at P20 (Figure 3C–C'') and P10 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: SOX9 showed strong expression throughout the IVD in littermate control mouse spine at P20 and P10.
source: We assayed SOX9, an essential transcriptional regulator of cartilage and IVD homeostasis in mouse (Henry et al., 2012), which showed strong expression throughout the IVD in littermate control mouse spine at P20 (Figure 3C–C'') and P10 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3C-C'' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice showed reduced SOX9 expression throughout the IVD at P20 in both scoliotic and non-scoliotic mutant mice.
source: In contrast, Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice showed reduced SOX9 expression throughout the IVD at P20 in both scoliotic and non-scoliotic mutant mice (Figure 3D–D'', G).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3D-D'', G.

claim: SOX9 expression is not reduced in the IVD of P10 Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice.
source: Interestingly, SOX9 expression is not reduced in the IVD of P10 mutant mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J, L), suggesting that loss of SOX9 expression in the IVD is associated with the initiation of scoliosis.
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J, L.

claim: Loss of SOX9 expression in the IVD is associated with the initiation of scoliosis.
source: Interestingly, SOX9 expression is not reduced in the IVD of P10 mutant mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J, L), suggesting that loss of SOX9 expression in the IVD is associated with the initiation of scoliosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of SOX9 reduction coinciding with scoliosis onset.

claim: SOX9 directly regulates type II collagen (COLII) expression.
source: SOX9 directly regulates type II collagen (COLII) expression (Bell et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: COLII shows a concentration gradient of high expression in the nucleus pulposus, decreasing outwards in the annulus fibrosus.
source: Analysis of COLII expression in the IVD shows a concentration gradient of high expression in the nucleus pulposus, decreasing the annulus fibrosus outwards, while type I collagen (COLI) is primarily expressed in the annulus fibrosus (Beard et al., 1980; Mader et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Type I collagen (COLI) is primarily expressed in the annulus fibrosus.
source: Analysis of COLII expression in the IVD shows a concentration gradient of high expression in the nucleus pulposus, decreasing the annulus fibrosus outwards, while type I collagen (COLI) is primarily expressed in the annulus fibrosus (Beard et al., 1980; Mader et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Regular expression of COLII was observed in the IVDs at P20 regardless of genotype.
source: We observed regular expression of COLII in the IVDs at P20 regardless of genotype (Figure 3E, F); however, the typical distribution of COLI-positive (COLI+) cells was altered Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice with scoliosis (Figure 3H–M).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: The typical distribution of COLI-positive cells was altered in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice with scoliosis.
source: We observed regular expression of COLII in the IVDs at P20 regardless of genotype (Figure 3E, F); however, the typical distribution of COLI-positive (COLI+) cells was altered Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice with scoliosis (Figure 3H–M).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3H-M.

claim: In control IVDs, COLI+ cells are observed in the inner annulus fibrosus and sparsely in the cartilaginous endplate.
source: In control IVDs, COLI+ cells are observed in the inner annulus fibrosus and sparsely in the cartilaginous endplate (red arrows, Figure 3H–J).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3H-J.

claim: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutants showed a reduction in COLI+ cells in the inner annulus fibrosus at the convex side of the curvature.
source: However, Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutants showed a reduction in COLI+ cells in the inner annulus fibrosus at the convex side of the curvature (Figure 3K), concomitant with increased COLI+ cells in the inner annulus fibrosus on the concave side (red arrows, Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutants showed increased COLI+ cells in the inner annulus fibrosus on the concave side.
source: However, Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutants showed a reduction in COLI+ cells in the inner annulus fibrosus at the convex side of the curvature (Figure 3K), concomitant with increased COLI+ cells in the inner annulus fibrosus on the concave side (red arrows, Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The growth plate consistently showed increased COLI+ cells in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.
source: Interestingly, the growth plate consistently showed increased COLI+ cells in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice (green arrows, Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: No significant changes in GAG quantity or alterations in specific GAG species were observed in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant IVDs at P20.
source: We utilized Strong-Anion-Exchange high-pressure liquid chromatography (SAX-HPLC) to quantify proteoglycan species within the IVDs isolated from Cre (-) control and Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice at P20. The main GAG species detected are various chondroitin sulfate (CS) species and a minor amount of hyaluronan (HA) species. However, we observed no significant changes in GAG quantity or alterations in specific GAG species (Supplementary file 1), demonstrating that loss of Adgrg6 did not alter the expression of a significant class of proteoglycan species in the IVD at the initiation of scoliosis.
evidence: This is supported by SAX-HPLC data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Loss of Adgrg6 did not alter the expression of a significant class of proteoglycan species in the IVD at the initiation of scoliosis.
source: However, we observed no significant changes in GAG quantity or alterations in specific GAG species (Supplementary file 1), demonstrating that loss of Adgrg6 did not alter the expression of a significant class of proteoglycan species in the IVD at the initiation of scoliosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GAG analysis data.

claim: Minor alterations in SOX9 expression in the postnatal IVD of mice may be sufficient to initiate biomechanical instability leading to disc wedging and driving the onset of spine curvature.
source: In summary, these results show that loss of Adgrg6 in osteochondral progenitor cells leads to alterations in the typical expression pattern of SOX9+ and COLI+ cells within the IVDs. In contrast, alterations of bulk ECM components, including COLII and GAG proteoglycans, were not significantly affected at the onset of scoliosis, suggesting that even minor alterations in SOX9 expression in the postnatal IVD of mice may be sufficient to initiate biomechanical instability leading to disc wedging and driving the onset of spine curvature, without grossly affecting tissue architecture and composition of the major ECM components of the IVD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that SOX9 is reduced while major ECM components are not significantly altered.

claim: ADGRG6 has an established role for control of cAMP signaling in other contexts.
source: Next, we set out to understand how ADGRG6 regulates the homeostasis of the IVD. Given the established role of ADGRG6 for control of cAMP signaling in other contexts (Geng et al., 2013; Monk et al., 2009; Monk et al., 2011), we first analyzed the expression pattern of Serine-133 phosphorylated CREB (pCREB)—the active form of cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB)—in spine tissues.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: pCREB expression is typically enriched throughout cartilaginous elements of the spine, including the cartilaginous endplate and nucleus pulposus.
source: pCREB expression is typically enriched throughout cartilaginous elements of the spine, including the cartilaginous endplate and nucleus pulposus (Figure 4A–A'', C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, G').
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4A-A'', C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G-G'.

claim: pCREB is expressed in some cells of the periosteum.
source: It is also expressed in some cells of the periosteum (Figure 4A''', C).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4A''', C.

claim: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice showed a decrease in pCREB+ cells in cartilaginous tissues at P20.
source: In contrast, Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice showed a decrease in pCREB+ cells in these tissues at P20 (Figure 4B–B''', C), indicating that Adgrg6 is essential for regulating pCREB expression in cartilaginous tissues of the spine.
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4B-B''', C.

claim: Adgrg6 is essential for regulating pCREB expression in cartilaginous tissues of the spine.
source: In contrast, Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice showed a decrease in pCREB+ cells in these tissues at P20 (Figure 4B–B''', C), indicating that Adgrg6 is essential for regulating pCREB expression in cartilaginous tissues of the spine.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in pCREB in mutant mice.

claim: IHC showed reduced pCREB expression in the nucleus pulposus in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutants at P10.
source: Furthermore, IHC showed reduced pCREB expression in the nucleus pulposus in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutants at P10 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H, H', K), suggesting that alteration of CREB signaling emerges before the initiation of scoliosis.
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-H', K.

claim: Alteration of CREB signaling emerges before the initiation of scoliosis in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.
source: Furthermore, IHC showed reduced pCREB expression in the nucleus pulposus in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutants at P10 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H, H', K), suggesting that alteration of CREB signaling emerges before the initiation of scoliosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of pCREB reduction at P10 before scoliosis onset at P20.

claim: Adgrg6 knockout ATDC5 cells displayed global disruptions of typical chondrogenic gene expression.
source: We previously demonstrated that Adgrg6 knockout (KO) ATDC5 chondrogenic cells displayed global disruptions of typical chondrogenic gene expression (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Adgrg6 KO ATDC5 cells showed reduced pCREB compared with unedited control cells.
source: In agreement with our findings in the IVD, we show reduced pCREB in Adgrg6 KO ATDC5 cells compared with unedited control cells (n = 5 biological repeats) (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: ADGRG6 can signal through Gs/cAMP in other contexts.
source: Given that ADGRG6 can signal through Gs/cAMP in other contexts (Geng et al., 2013; Mogha et al., 2013; Monk et al., 2009), we next asked whether treatment with Forskolin (FSK), a small molecule activator of the adenylyl cyclase, could restore pCREB expression independent of ADGRG6 function in ATDC5 cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Addition of FSK to ATDC5 cell culture stimulated pCREB expression in both ATDC5 WT cells and Adgrg6 KO cells.
source: Western analysis showed that the addition of FSK to ATDC5 cell culture could stimulate pCREB expression in both ATDC5 WT cells and Adgrg6 KO cells, albeit at a reduced level of expression after FSK treatment in Adgrg6 KO cells (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: FSK treatment stimulated pCREB expression at a reduced level in Adgrg6 KO cells compared to WT cells.
source: Western analysis showed that the addition of FSK to ATDC5 cell culture could stimulate pCREB expression in both ATDC5 WT cells and Adgrg6 KO cells, albeit at a reduced level of expression after FSK treatment in Adgrg6 KO cells (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Loss of Adgrg6 in cartilaginous tissues of the spine led to increased hypertrophy and expression of type X collagen in cartilaginous endplate and growth plate.
source: Loss of Adgrg6 in cartilaginous tissues of the spine led to increased hypertrophy and expression of type X collagen (encoded by Col10a1) in cartilaginous endplate and growth plate (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CREB signaling is associated with reduced Col10a1 expression in primary growth plate chondrocytes.
source: CREB signaling is associated with reduced Col10a1expression in primary growth plate chondrocytes (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Asymmetric expression of type X collagen in vertebral growth plates has been observed in AIS patient samples.
source: Interestingly, asymmetric expression of type X collagen in vertebral growth plates has been observed in AIS patient samples (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical study.

claim: Treatment of ATDC5 cells with a low concentration of FSK (2 µM) for 7 days restored typical expression of Col10a1 in Adgrg6 KO cells.
source: We found that treatment of ATDC5 cells with a low concentration of FSK (2 µM) for 7 days restored typical expression of Col10a1 and partially restored Sox9 expression in Adgrg6 KO cells (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Treatment of ATDC5 cells with FSK (2 µM) for 7 days partially restored Sox9 expression in Adgrg6 KO cells.
source: We found that treatment of ATDC5 cells with a low concentration of FSK (2 µM) for 7 days restored typical expression of Col10a1 and partially restored Sox9 expression in Adgrg6 KO cells (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of Acan and Col2a1 in Adgrg6 KO cells was not restored by FSK treatment.
source: However, the expression of other affected genes, such as decreased expression of Acan and Col2a1 in Adgrg6 KO cells, was not restored by this approach (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adgrg6 is necessary for cAMP-driven CREB signaling in several cartilaginous tissues for the regulation of a subset of essential genes involved in the homeostasis of the IVD.
source: Taken together, these results support a model where Adgrg6 is necessary for cAMP-driven CREB signaling in several cartilaginous tissues for the regulation of a subset of essential genes involved in the homeostasis of the IVD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined results of pCREB reduction and FSK rescue experiments.

claim: Abnormal bone quality or osteopenia is frequently associated with AIS.
source: Abnormal bone quality or osteopenia is frequently associated with AIS (Cheng et al., 2000; Cheng et al., 2001; Lam et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: All Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice showed straight spine alignment at P40 and P120.
source: To examine whether alterations could further explain scoliosis in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice in bone quality, we generated Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice. All Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice we assayed showed straight spine alignment at P40 and P120 (n = 8) (Figure 5C, E), which was typical of both Cre (-) or Cre (+) littermate controls (Figure 5A, B, D).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Similar results were observed in Sp7Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.
source: Similar results were observed in Sp7Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice in which Adgrg6 was ablated in committed osteoblast precursors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, n = 9).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MicroCT analyses revealed typical architecture of the vertebral bodies and comparable bone mass in the thoracic spines of both Cre (-) control and Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice at P120.
source: Micro-computed tomography (microCT) analyses revealed the typical architecture of the vertebral bodies and comparable bone mass in the thoracic spines of both Cre (-) control and Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice at P120 (Figure 5F–I), which was confirmed by the bone volume analysis (BV/TV) on both control and mutant vertebral bodies (Figure 5J, n = 4 for each group).
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figure 5F-J.

claim: No histopathological changes of the vertebral bodies or IVDs were observed in Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice at P120.
source: We did not observe histopathological changes of the vertebral bodies or IVDs of the Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice at P120 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Real-time RT-PCR analyses revealed very low expression of Adgrg6 in the Cre (-) control sample compared with the expression of Col1a1.
source: Real-time RT-PCR analyses revealed very low expression of Adgrg6 in the Cre (-) control sample compared with the expression of Col1a1 (0.2% expression of Col1a1), which is the most abundant collagen expressed in bone (Long, 2012; Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: The expression of Adgrg6 was significantly reduced (~71%) in Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.
source: However, the expression of Adgrg6 was significantly reduced (~71%) in Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Adgrg6 has no apparent role in mature osteoblasts during postnatal bone mass accrual or homeostasis.
source: These results show that Adgrg6 has no apparent role in mature osteoblasts during postnatal bone mass accrual or homeostasis and that alterations in bone quality are not driving scoliosis in the Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f AIS mouse model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of phenotype in Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.

claim: Alterations in bone quality are not driving scoliosis in the Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f AIS mouse model.
source: These results show that Adgrg6 has no apparent role in mature osteoblasts during postnatal bone mass accrual or homeostasis and that alterations in bone quality are not driving scoliosis in the Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f AIS mouse model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of phenotype in Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.

claim: Embryonic induction of ATC from E0.5-P20 leads to complete recombination in cartilaginous tissues of the IVD.
source: Interestingly, we consistently observed retention of ADGRG6 expression in some regions of the inner annulus fibrosis of the ATC; Adgrg6f/f mice induced from P1–P20 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, D') compared with the mutants induced from P0.5–P20 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, B'), suggesting that embryonic induction leads to complete recombination in cartilaginous tissues of the IVD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of ADGRG6 expression between different induction strategies.

claim: Ablation of Adgrg6 during embryonic development resulted in 25% and 16.7% of ATC; Adgrg6f/f mice showing scoliosis at P20 and P180, respectively.
source: Ablation of Adgrg6 during embryonic development resulted in 25% (n = 16) and 16.7% (n = 12) of ATC; Adgrg6f/f mice showing scoliosis at P20 and P180, respectively (Figure 6A–C, H).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray and Cobb angle data shown in Figure 6A-C, H.

claim: Cobb angle measurements revealed curve severity between 11° and 43° in scoliotic ATC; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice.
source: Cobb angle measurements revealed curve severity between 11° and 43° in scoliotic mutant mice (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by Cobb angle data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Ablation of Adgrg6 during perinatal development in ATC; Adgrg6f/f mice showed no evidence of scoliosis at P20.
source: Ablation of Adgrg6 during perinatal development in ATC; Adgrg6f/f mice showed no evidence of scoliosis when assayed at P20 (0.0%; n = 8), while a single ATC; Adgrg6f/f mutant mouse (12.5%; n = 8) showed late-onset scoliosis when assayed at P180 with a curve of 23.8° (Figure 6D–F, J).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray and Cobb angle data shown in Figure 6D-F, J.

claim: A single ATC; Adgrg6f/f mutant mouse (12.5%) showed late-onset scoliosis at P180 with a curve of 23.8° when Adgrg6 was ablated during perinatal development.
source: Ablation of Adgrg6 during perinatal development in ATC; Adgrg6f/f mice showed no evidence of scoliosis when assayed at P20 (0.0%; n = 8), while a single ATC; Adgrg6f/f mutant mouse (12.5%; n = 8) showed late-onset scoliosis when assayed at P180 with a curve of 23.8° (Figure 6D–F, J).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray and Cobb angle data shown in Figure 6D-F, J.

claim: None of the Cre (-) littermate control mice showed spine deformity at P20 or P180.
source: None of the Cre (-) littermate control mice showed spine deformity at P20 or P180 (Figure 6G, I).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray and Cobb angle data shown in Figure 6G, I.

claim: Loss of Adgrg6 in committed cartilages of the axial skeletal is sufficient to generate a mild susceptibility to scoliosis, although with a much lower penetrance compared with removal of Adgrg6 in the whole spine.
source: Altogether, this suggested that loss of Adgrg6 in committed cartilages of the axial skeletal is sufficient to generate a mild susceptibility to scoliosis, although with a much lower penetrance compared with removal of Adgrg6 in the whole spine (i.e., Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f) (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of scoliosis penetrance between ATC; Adgrg6f/f and Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.

claim: The pathogenesis of AIS is the result of tissue-level defects, which accumulate during embryonic development.
source: These results suggest that the pathogenesis of AIS is the result of tissue-level defects, which accumulate during embryonic development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that embryonic deletion of Adgrg6 increases scoliosis penetrance.

claim: Perinatal induction (P1-P5) in Col2a1-CreERT2; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ mice led to near-complete recombination in cells of the cartilaginous endplate, vertebral growth plate, and most cells of the inner annulus fibrosus but not the outer annulus fibrosus.
source: β-Galactosidase staining of spine sections of Col2a1-CreERT2; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ mice at P28 showed that perinatal induction (P1–P5) led to near-complete recombination in cells of the cartilaginous endplate, vertebral growth plate, and most cells of the inner annulus fibrosus but not the outer annulus fibrosus (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, A'), similar to the recombination profile of ATC (Figure 1I–J'), except that Col2a1-CreERT2 did not target the nucleus pulposus (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-A'.

claim: Col2a1-CreERT2 did not target the nucleus pulposus.
source: β-Galactosidase staining of spine sections of Col2a1-CreERT2; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ mice at P28 showed that perinatal induction (P1–P5) led to near-complete recombination in cells of the cartilaginous endplate, vertebral growth plate, and most cells of the inner annulus fibrosus but not the outer annulus fibrosus (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, A'), similar to the recombination profile of ATC (Figure 1I–J'), except that Col2a1-CreERT2 did not target the nucleus pulposus (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Postnatal induction (P14-P18) in Col2a1-CreERT2; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ mice only led to partial recombination within endplate and growth plate, and some cells of the inner annulus fibrosus.
source: Unfortunately, postnatal induction (P14–P18) in Col2a1-CreERT2; Rosa26-lsl-lacZ mice only led to partial recombination within endplate and growth plate, and some cells of the inner annulus fibrosus, while the outer annulus fibrosus and nucleus pulposus were not targeted (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, B').
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B-B'.

claim: No scoliosis was observed in Col2a1-CreERT2; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice after perinatal induction (P1-P5) at P30.
source: We did not observe scoliosis in Col2a1-CreERT2; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice after perinatal induction (P1–P5) at P30 (0.0%; n = 8) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, C', J).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray and Cobb angle data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-C', J.

claim: A single (14.3%) Col2a1-CreERT2; Adgrg6f/f mouse presented with very mild, late-onset scoliosis (12.4°) at P90 after perinatal induction (P1-P5).
source: However, a single (14.3%; n = 7) Col2a1-CreERT2; Adgrg6f/f mice presented with very mild, late-onset scoliosis (12.4°) at P90 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D', J).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray and Cobb angle data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D', J.

claim: No evidence of scoliosis was found in Col2a1-CreERT2; Adgrg6f/f mice induced at P14-P18 at either P30 or P90.
source: We also found no evidence of scoliosis in Col2a1-CreERT2; Adgrg6f/f mice induced at P14–P18 at either P30 or P90 (0.0%; n = 5 for Col2a1-CreERT2; Adgrg6f/f and 0.0%; n = 4 for controls, respectively) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F–H, K, L).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray and Cobb angle data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F-H, K, L.

claim: Adgrg6 plays only a minor role in the postnatal regulation of cartilaginous tissues for maintaining spine alignment in the mouse.
source: Altogether, our results confirmed that Adgrg6 plays only a minor role in the postnatal regulation of cartilaginous tissues for maintaining spine alignment in the mouse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low penetrance of scoliosis with postnatal deletion of Adgrg6.

claim: There was a slight increase in the incidence of scoliosis in the ATC; Adgrg6f/f mice with embryonic deletion of Adgrg6 compared to perinatal deletion.
source: However, we showed a slight increase in the incidence of scoliosis in the ATC; Adgrg6f/f mice with embryonic deletion of Adgrg6 compared to perinatal deletion.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of scoliosis incidence data between different induction strategies.

claim: The contributions of cartilaginous elements for spine alignment are established during embryonic development in the mouse.
source: These results further support a model where the contributions of cartilaginous elements for spine alignment are established during embryonic development in the mouse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that embryonic deletion has higher penetrance than postnatal deletion.

claim: Connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers–Danlos and Marfan syndromes display scoliosis as a common symptom.
source: Connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers–Danlos and Marfan syndromes display scoliosis as a common symptom (Hoffjan, 2012) and generalized joint hypermobility is a risk factor for developing AIS (Haller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Generalized joint hypermobility is a risk factor for developing AIS.
source: Connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers–Danlos and Marfan syndromes display scoliosis as a common symptom (Hoffjan, 2012) and generalized joint hypermobility is a risk factor for developing AIS (Haller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical study.

claim: Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice were indistinguishable from littermate controls at birth.
source: To address a specific role of Adgrg6 in dense connective tissues of the spine, we generated Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice, which were indistinguishable from littermate controls at birth.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: 55.6% of Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice exhibited scoliosis at P120, with curve severity ranged between 12° and 30°.
source: Longitudinal X-ray analyses revealed that 55.6% (n = 9) of Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice exhibited scoliosis at P120, with curve severity ranged between 12° and 30° (Figure 7B, B', F).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray and Cobb angle data shown in Figure 7B-B', F.

claim: None of the Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice showed scoliosis at P40.
source: Interestingly, none of these mice showed scoliosis at P40 (n = 9) (Figure 7A, A' , F).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray and Cobb angle data shown in Figure 7A-A', F.

claim: No scoliosis was observed in Cre (-) or Cre (+) littermate control mice at either P40 or P120.
source: No scoliosis was observed in Cre (-) or Cre (+) littermate control mice at either P40 or P120 (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray data shown in Figure 7C-E.

claim: Histological analysis revealed some mildly wedged IVDs and shifted nucleus pulposus within the scoliotic curve of the Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant spine at P120.
source: Histological analysis revealed some mildly wedged IVDs and shifted nucleus pulposus within the scoliotic curve of the Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant spine at P120 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), with IVDs outside of the curve region displaying typical morphology (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Dense connective tissues of the spine are essential for maintaining spine alignment later during adult development (after P40).
source: Altogether, this demonstrates that dense connective tissues of the spine are essential for maintaining spine alignment later during adult development (after P40) and may act synergistically with the IVD to promote typical spine alignment during postnatal development in the mouse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the late-onset scoliosis in Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.

claim: Dense connective tissues may act synergistically with the IVD to promote typical spine alignment during postnatal development in the mouse.
source: Altogether, this demonstrates that dense connective tissues of the spine are essential for maintaining spine alignment later during adult development (after P40) and may act synergistically with the IVD to promote typical spine alignment during postnatal development in the mouse.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the combined observations from different mutant models.

claim: The total cross-sectional area was increased in Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f tendons compared to Cre (-) controls.
source: We found that the total cross-sectional area was increased in Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f tendons compared to Cre (-) controls (p=0.0037) (Figure 7G–I).
evidence: This is supported by mechanical testing data shown in Figure 7G-I.

claim: Deletion of Adgrg6 resulted in mechanically weaker tendons with reduced elastic moduli.
source: Micromechanical tensile testing revealed that deletion of Adgrg6 resulted in mechanically weaker tendons with reduced elastic moduli (p=0.0395) and a trend of reduced failure stresses (p=0.0589) (Figure 7K, N).
evidence: This is supported by mechanical testing data shown in Figure 7K, N.

claim: Deletion of Adgrg6 showed a trend of reduced failure stresses in tendons.
source: Micromechanical tensile testing revealed that deletion of Adgrg6 resulted in mechanically weaker tendons with reduced elastic moduli (p=0.0395) and a trend of reduced failure stresses (p=0.0589) (Figure 7K, N).
evidence: This is supported by mechanical testing data shown in Figure 7K, N.

claim: No differences in failure force or failure strain were observed in Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f tendons.
source: We observed no differences in failure force or failure strain (Figure 7L, M).
evidence: This is supported by mechanical testing data shown in Figure 7L-M.

claim: Ablation of Adgrg6 in Scx-expressing cells compromises the biomechanical properties of dense connective tissues, which likely contributes to the pathogenesis of late-onset scoliosis in Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.
source: This data suggests that ablation of Adgrg6 in Scx-expressing cells compromises the biomechanical properties of dense connective tissues, which likely contributes to the pathogenesis of late-onset scoliosis in Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanical testing results and scoliosis phenotype.

claim: ADGRG6 has a tissue-level function within the cartilaginous tissues and dense connective tissue of the spine for the maintenance of homeostatic signaling and biomechanical properties to regulate postnatal spine alignment in the mouse.
source: Altogether, this study demonstrates the essential role of ADGRG6 and its tissue-level function within the cartilaginous tissues and dense connective tissue of the spine and highlights its role in the maintenance of homeostatic signaling and biomechanical properties of these spine elements to regulate postnatal spine alignment in the mouse.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice are a unique genetic model of AIS, with construct validity.
source: We suggest that Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice are a unique genetic model of AIS, with construct validity (Willner, 1984).

Therefore, our observations suggest that embryonic deletion of Adgrg6 leads to subtle structural or biomechanical changes of these structural elements of the spine, which in turn may lead to increased susceptibility of scoliosis during periods of rapid skeletal growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.
